issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Kiet Nguyen, a 44-year-old nurse at a county hospital, had always been steady on his feet—until the night he was mugged three months ago. After a double shift, he walked toward the parking garage through a poorly lit alley, when a man grabbed him from behind, pressed a knife against his ribs, and snarled for his wallet. Kiet handed it over, but the man punched him hard in the jaw before disappearing. The metallic pain, the flash of the blade, the helpless freeze—these details were not just memories; they were photographic images that replayed in his mind with perfect clarity, and whenever they returned he felt the same sharp ache in his jaw, as if the blow were landing again. This vivid recall convinced him that he had failed somehow, that there must be something about him that had drawn the attack. He began to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that his future had evaporated in that alley. The certainty that his future was gone kept pulling him back into the alley, replaying the moment over and over, as if to confirm what he already knew.

That conviction drove everything that followed. Kiet started to scan every corridor he walked, checking behind him before entering any room, and choosing seats in the staff break room that faced the door with his back firmly against the wall. He also kept his mind deliberately occupied—listening to podcasts during his commute, replaying surgical procedures in his head, anything to prevent the images from intruding. Yet these very strategies seemed to keep the memory alive: when he scanned his surroundings, he would catch the silhouette of a tall man and his heart would lurch, triggering the photographic recall again. When he checked the mirrors in the hospital restroom to make sure no one was behind him, he caught his own reflection and thought, *You should have seen it coming*—reinforcing his sense of intrinsic fault. The more he tried to control his environment, the more he felt that nothing good was possible, tightening the loop of hopelessness. Having come to believe that he was fundamentally marked for misfortune, Kiet now saw danger in even familiar spaces—the hospital corridor he had walked for years suddenly felt like an ambush waiting to happen.

Sleep became elusive. Kiet would lie awake for hours, listening for footsteps, convinced that someone was moving through his apartment. He started sleeping with the bedroom door locked and a chair wedged under the knob—a futile gesture that only reminded him of how unsafe he actually was. During the day, even a routine walk to the hospital pharmacy required a mental safety rehearsal: he would glance over his shoulder repeatedly, pick a path with clear sightlines, and avoid any corner he could not see around. Each time he looked behind him, the memory of the robber’s approach surged back—the knife, the voice, the pain. And each time he felt that helpless flash, his appraisal deepened: *There is nothing good ahead. I have no future.* The threat he perceived was not just external; it confirmed his hopelessness, and his hopelessness sharpened his vigilance, so that a stranger walking too close on the sidewalk sent him into a full replay of the assault.

At work, Kiet’s constant checking became noticeable. A colleague remarked that he seemed jumpy, and he laughed it off, but privately he believed that if he stopped watching, something terrible would happen again—because he was the kind of person who drew bad events. His avoidance of the parking garage meant he now parked three blocks away, adding to his exhaustion. He had come to see the mugging as a punishment for a flaw he could not name, and the only way to manage the dread was to stay hyperaware. But that hyperawareness only fed the memories, and the memories fed his certainty that there was no point in planning for tomorrow.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a morning when he found himself weeping silently while brushing his teeth, the face of the robber superimposed over his own in the mirror. He had spent months trying to outrun a memory that now felt like the only thing that was real. He was terrified that the hopelessness would never lift, that he would spend the rest of his life looking over his shoulder. But he also, somewhere beneath the dread, wanted to believe that a future might still exist—if only he could find a way to stop seeing the alley every time he closed his eyes.
